content.title: About
content.content: Low‑fat chocolate milk (1 % fat) is a beverage made from skimmed cow’s milk, cocoa powder, and sweetener. It retains the creamy taste and nutritional profile of milk while providing far less fat than regular chocolate milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Low‑fat chocolate milk is popular in sports nutrition because it offers high protein with low calories.
Cocoa powder adds flavonoid antioxidants that may support cardiovascular health.
In many markets the drink is fortified with vitamin D and calcium to offset the loss of fat‑soluble nutrients.
Sugar levels are often reduced compared with full‑fat versions, but sweeteners are added to keep the chocolate flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A typical serving provides about 8 g of high‑quality milk protein, supporting muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: With roughly 50 kcal per 100 ml, it fits well into weight‑management plans.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Despite the low fat, the drink remains a good source of calcium for bone health, often fortified with vitamin D for better absorption.

items.title: Cocoa antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids in cocoa may reduce oxidative stress and improve vascular function.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Milk contains electrolytes such as potassium and sodium, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: As a dairy product, it can cause discomfort for people who cannot digest lactose.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey should avoid this beverage.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: Some versions contain added sugars; those monitoring blood glucose should check the label.

items.title: Vitamin fortification
items.content: Excessive consumption of fortified drinks may lead to vitamin A or D overdose.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Low‑fat chocolate milk can be enjoyed as a refreshing drink, blended into smoothies, used as a base for protein shakes, or poured over oatmeal, pancakes, and cereal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. Do not freeze, as it may alter texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Rockstar is an energy drink containing caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and sugar (or its substitutes). It is designed to boost energy, improve focus and reduce fatigue during intense physical and mental activities.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Rockstar brand was founded in 2001 in the United States and quickly became a market leader in energy drinks.
The formula often includes guarana extract, which adds an extra energy kick.
Rockstar is available in more than 30 flavors, including original, berry, tropical and sugar‑free versions.
The company actively supports extreme sports, sponsoring skateboarding, BMX and CrossFit events.
In some countries the drink is sold as “Zero” – sugar‑free but with the same caffeine level.

items.title: Increased alertness
items.content: Caffeine and taurine stimulate the central nervous system, enhancing attention and reaction time.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: B‑vitamins help convert food into usable energy.

items.title: Improved physical endurance
items.content: The combination of sugar (or substitutes) and stimulants can speed up recovery after intense workouts.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High doses may cause anxiety, insomnia, rapid heartbeat and increased blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sugared versions can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries with frequent consumption.

items.title: Not suitable for children and pregnant women
items.content: Due to its high caffeine level, the drink is not recommended for people under 18, pregnant or nursing women.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of certain stimulants and antidepressants.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Chill the drink and consume in small servings (200–250 ml) before training, during work, or when feeling fatigued. Do not exceed 2–3 servings per day.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, it is best consumed within 30 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Honey is a sweet, viscous liquid that bees make from flower nectar. It consists mostly of sugars (about 80%) and water. Its color, aroma, and flavor depend on the plants the nectar came from: it can be light acacia, fragrant linden, or dark buckwheat. Honey is eaten as a treat and added to tea, baked goods, dressings, and marinades.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bees visit millions of flowers to make a kilogram of honey.
Honey is about 80% sugars, mainly glucose and fructose.
Over time honey may crystallize, which is a natural process and not spoilage.
The color and flavor of honey depend on the plants: acacia, linden, buckwheat, sunflower, and others.
When stored properly, honey practically does not spoil.

items.title: Source of energy
items.content: Honey provides quick energy thanks to glucose and fructose.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic acids and flavonoids in honey have antioxidant properties; darker varieties usually have more.

items.title: May soothe a cough
items.content: A spoonful of honey may help with a cough in adults and children over one year old.

items.title: Antibacterial properties
items.content: Medical-grade honey is used in the care of some wounds, but these are special sterile products.

items.title: Adds flavor and sweetness
items.content: Honey is sweeter than sugar, so a smaller amount may be enough for taste.

items.title: Not for infants under one year
items.content: Honey should not be given to children under one year old because of the risk of infant botulism.

items.title: Sugar and calories
items.content: Honey is mostly sugar: it is high in calories and can harm teeth, and people with diabetes need to count it in their diet.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: In people allergic to pollen or bee products, honey can trigger a reaction.

items.title: Quality and counterfeits
items.content: Honey is sometimes diluted with syrup, so it is better to buy from trusted producers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat honey by the spoonful, or add it to warm tea, bread, porridge, yogurt, baked goods, dressings, and marinades. Do not put it in boiling water; wait until the drink cools slightly. Honey is added sugar, so keep the amount moderate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store honey in a tightly closed jar at room temperature in a dry place away from direct light. In the refrigerator it crystallizes faster. Crystallized honey can be gently warmed in a water bath. If honey foams or smells sour, it may have fermented and is best discarded.

content.title: About
content.content: Sheep milk is a thick, rich milk with a mild, slightly sweet flavor. It contains more fat, protein, and total solids than cow and goat milk. Sheep milk is drunk less often and is used mostly for cheeses, such as Roquefort, pecorino, feta, and ricotta, and for yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sheep milk is thicker and fattier than cow milk, so it yields more cheese and yogurt.
Sheep milk is made into Roquefort, Pecorino Romano, feta, Manchego, and ricotta.
A sheep gives far less milk than a cow.
Sheep give milk seasonally, most often in spring and summer.
Yogurt made from sheep milk is especially thick and creamy.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Sheep milk has a lot of protein, which muscles and tissues need.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: It usually has more calcium than cow milk.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin
items.content: These vitamins support metabolism and the formation of blood cells.

items.title: Contains zinc and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals support immunity and bone health.

items.title: Contains medium-chain fatty acids
items.content: Sheep milk fat is rich in these fatty acids.

items.title: Calories and saturated fat
items.content: Sheep milk is fatty and high in calories, so portions should be moderate, especially with high cholesterol.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: Sheep milk contains lactose, so it is not suitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: With an allergy to cow milk proteins, sheep milk is usually unsafe too because of cross-reaction.

items.title: Raw milk
items.content: Raw milk may contain Brucella, Campylobacter, and Listeria; it should be boiled or drunk pasteurized.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink sheep milk pasteurized or boiled, add it to porridge and baked goods, or more often use it for yogurt, cottage cheese, and cheeses. Because of its richness, it is sometimes diluted or used in small amounts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store milk in the refrigerator in a closed container and use it by the date on the package; after opening, within a few days. Sheep milk freezes well. Discard milk that smells sour.

content.title: About
content.content: Split peas are dried halves of peas that have had vegetable fat added to improve flavor and mouthfeel. They are commonly used in soups, purees, and side dishes. Dried peas are a rich source of plant protein, complex carbohydrates, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Split peas cook faster than whole peas – usually 20‑30 minutes.
The added fat raises the calorie count and gives a creamy texture without extra butter.
Peas belong to the legume family and are an excellent plant‑based protein source.
In some cultures split peas are a staple of traditional dishes, such as Scottish “potage”.
Dried peas have a long shelf life when stored in a cool, dry place.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: One cup of dried split peas provides about 16 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Peas raise blood sugar slowly, making them suitable for glycemic control.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, folate, and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, magnesium, phosphorus and zinc, supporting blood health and bones.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: High calorie content from added fat
items.content: The added fat increases energy density, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause flatulence in sensitive people; soaking and thorough cooking help.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Dried peas contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; heat treatment reduces it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook split peas in water or broth until tender, then use them in soups, stews, purees, or as a side dish. A splash of oil or a dollop of cream enhances flavor. Rinse and soak the peas for 4‑6 hours before cooking for best texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried split peas in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored they keep for 2‑3 years. After opening, watch for moisture and off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Tea with ginger is an aromatic beverage made from black (or green) tea leaves flavored with dried ginger. It combines the brisk taste of tea with the spicy warmth of ginger, making it popular both hot and cold.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ginger has been used in traditional Chinese and Indian medicine for over 5,000 years.
Tea and ginger pair is common in Asian cultures, where ginger tea is considered a warming drink.
Ginger tea is often served with honey or lemon to enhance flavor and benefits.
Dried ginger retains most of its active compounds, including gingerol.
In some countries ginger tea is sold in ready‑to‑use tea bags, while in others it is offered as loose leaf.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Ginger has anti‑inflammatory and antioxidant properties that may help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Improved digestion
items.content: Ginger stimulates gastric secretions, aiding the digestion of food.

items.title: Nausea relief
items.content: Warm ginger tea is commonly recommended for motion sickness, morning sickness, and postoperative nausea.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine from tea combined with ginger’s aroma can improve focus and increase alertness.

items.title: Blood sugar moderation
items.content: Studies suggest ginger may help modestly lower post‑meal glucose levels.

items.title: Ginger allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to ginger, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Ginger can enhance the effects of anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin) and increase bleeding risk.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: High amounts of ginger may irritate the stomach lining, causing heartburn or discomfort.

items.title: Pregnancy
items.content: Pregnant women should limit ginger intake to no more than 1 g per day unless advised by a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steep 1‑2 teaspoons of ginger tea in 250 ml of hot water for 3‑5 minutes. Add honey, lemon, or milk if desired. It can be enjoyed hot or chilled.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bagged or loose tea in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep dried ginger separately in a tightly sealed jar.
